stories.title: Four Months Old, This Bridge Shook Itself To Pieces
stories.description: The 1940 Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened on 1 July and tore itself apart on 7 November in a wind of about 40 mph. Engineers later traced it to aeroelastic flutter, not the resonance most textbooks still blame, and the only casualty was a cocker spaniel. #unsolvedmysteries #bizarrehistory #engineering

factual_claims.text: The 1940 Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened on 1 July 1940 and collapsed on 7 November 1940 in a wind of about 40 mph.
Construction workers nicknamed the bridge Galloping Gertie because its deck moved vertically in the wind.
On the morning of the collapse the deck's motion changed to a twisting torsional mode, with one side of the roadway rising as the other fell, and it fell at about 11:00 a.m.
The accepted explanation is aeroelastic flutter, a self-exciting unbounded torsional motion, and Theodore von Karman sat on the Federal Works Agency board that investigated the collapse.
No person died in the collapse; the only fatality was a cocker spaniel named Tubby, and the wreckage lies about 180 feet down and is on the National Register of Historic Places.

segments.narration: A new bridge tore itself apart in a forty-mile wind. Washington State, November 1940. Four months old.
The builders already called it Galloping Gertie. The deck rolled on ordinary days, and drivers crossed it for the ride.
That morning the roll became a twist. One lane climbed while the other dropped, and by eleven the span was in the water. Forty miles an hour. How does that beat steel?
It is called aeroelastic flutter. The wind fed the bridge's own twisting, and the twisting pulled in more energy than it shed. Theodore von Karman sat on the board that proved it.
Nobody died. A cocker spaniel named Tubby did. The wreck still lies a hundred and eighty feet down, now a protected reef.

research.summary: The first Tacoma Narrows Bridge, 2,800 ft main span and 5,939 ft overall, cost about 6.4 million dollars and opened 1 July 1940. Construction workers called it Galloping Gertie for its vertical deck motion. On 7 November 1940 swaying began around 9:45 a.m. and the main span fell at about 11:00 a.m. in a wind of roughly 40 mph (Farquharson recorded a 42 mph steady wind). The motion that destroyed it was torsional, not vertical. The modern explanation is aeroelastic flutter, a self-exciting and unbounded oscillation; the older forced-resonance account via Karman vortex shedding is wrong but survives in physics textbooks. A Federal Works Agency commission of Othmar Ammann, Theodore von Karman and Glenn B. Woodruff examined the failure. Leonard Coatsworth fled the deck and left his daughter's cocker spaniel Tubby in the car; the dog died and was the only fatality, with photographer Howard Clifford turning back from a rescue attempt. The wreckage sits about 180 ft deep, acts as an artificial reef and is on the National Register of Historic Places; cable and span steel was sold as scrap at a net loss of over 350,000 dollars, while the anchorages and tower pedestals were reused for the 1950 replacement.

stories.title: Soviet Maps Left Out The Town That Exploded
stories.description: On 29 September 1957 a tank of liquid nuclear waste exploded at the Mayak plant in the southern Urals, releasing an estimated 20 million curies. The closed city it happened in was not printed on any map, so the accident was named after the nearest town that was. #unsolvedmysteries #bizarrehistory #coldwar

factual_claims.text: On 29 September 1957 a tank of liquid high-level nuclear waste exploded at the Mayak plant in the southern Urals, and the Soviet Union concealed the accident.

Mayak was a plutonium reprocessing plant for Soviet nuclear weapons; a cooling system failure let the waste dry to ammonium nitrate and acetate residue, which exploded with a force of at least 70 tons of TNT.
About 2 million curies went into a plume spread over hundreds of kilometres, and evacuations only began on 6 October 1957, a week after the explosion.
The plant stood in the closed city of Chelyabinsk-40, which was not marked on maps, so the accident was named after Kyshtym, the nearest town that was.

An estimated 20 million curies was released in total, about 10,000 people were evacuated, the Soviet government only began declassifying the documents in 1989, and it remains the only accident rated INES level 6.

segments.narration: A tank of nuclear waste exploded and nobody was told. The southern Urals, September 1957.
Mayak made plutonium for Soviet bombs. One waste tank lost its cooling, baked itself dry, and went off with the force of seventy tonnes of TNT.
The blast threw a radioactive plume hundreds of kilometres downwind. Villagers kept working their fields for a week before anyone came to move them. How do you hide something that size?
You leave the town off the map. Chelyabinsk-40 was printed nowhere, so the accident got named after Kyshtym, the nearest place that officially existed.
Twenty million curies. Ten thousand people moved. No admission until 1989. It is still the only accident anywhere rated level six.

research.summary: On 29 September 1957 at 4:22 p.m. local time a tank holding 70-80 tons of liquid high-level waste at the Mayak plutonium reprocessing plant exploded. The tank's cooling system had failed and was not repaired; the waste evaporated and the dried residue, mainly ammonium nitrate and acetates, detonated with a force of at least 70 tons of TNT. An estimated 20 MCi (740 PBq) was released, about 2 MCi of it in a plume carried hundreds of kilometres, creating the East Ural Radioactive Trace over 800-20,000 square kilometres depending on threshold. Hot particles reached more than 52,000 square kilometres where at least 270,000 people lived; at least 22 villages were exposed and about 10,000 people were evacuated starting 6 October 1957, a week after the blast. The plant sat in the closed city of Chelyabinsk-40, now Ozyorsk, which was not shown on maps, so the accident took the name of Kyshtym, the nearest town that was. It is rated INES level 6, the only accident at that level. Western press carried vague reports from April 1958, Die Presse ran details on 18 March 1959, Zhores Medvedev made the scale known in 1976, and Soviet declassification began in 1989. In 1968 the East Ural Nature Reserve was created over the contaminated area.

factual_claims.text: When George Mallory's body was found on Everest his snow goggles were in his pocket rather than over his eyes.
Mallory and Sandy Irvine disappeared high on Everest on 8 June 1924 after Noel Odell's last sighting of them on the ridge.
Conrad Anker found Mallory's body on 1 May 1999 at 26,760 feet, with a rope still tied around his waist that had left crush and rope-jerk marks.

segments.narration: Mallory's snow goggles were in his pocket, not his eyes. Everest, and he had been missing for seventy-five years.
Mallory and Sandy Irvine went up on the eighth of June, 1924. Noel Odell watched two dots move on the ridge, then cloud closed.
Conrad Anker found him in 1999 just under twenty-seven thousand feet, a rope still knotted at his waist. Goggles come off when the light goes. So was he coming down from the top?
Probably not. The camera that would prove it was not on him, and neither was the photograph of his wife he meant to leave up there.
In 2024 a glacier far below gave up a boot with Irvine's name tape inside. The camera is still up there.

research.summary: George Mallory and Andrew 'Sandy' Irvine disappeared on the 1924 British Everest expedition; Wikipedia dates Mallory's death to 8 or 9 June 1924, and Noel Odell's last sighting placed them high on the ridge. On 1 May 1999 at about 11:45 a.m. Conrad Anker, with the Mallory and Irvine Research Expedition, found Mallory's body at 26,760 ft (8,156 m), prone with the head uphill, the right leg broken, the right elbow fractured or dislocated and ribs fractured. A rope tied at the waist had left crush injuries and rope-jerk marks, indicating the two were roped together at the accident. With the body were an altimeter by Cary of London with a broken crystal and no hands, a letter from 'Stella', meat lozenges, nail scissors, handkerchiefs, a pocketknife, matches and snow goggles; a Borgel wristwatch was recovered on 16 May. The Vest Pocket Kodak was not found despite a metal-detector sweep, and no photograph of his wife Ruth was on the body although his daughter said he planned to leave one on the summit. The goggles in his pocket suggest a descent in failing light or darkness; an alternative reading is that a blizzard between about 2 and 4 p.m. fogged the lenses. There is no conclusive evidence of a summit. In October 2024 a National Geographic team led by Jimmy Chin found a boot, sock with an 'A. C. Irvine' name tape, and a foot on the Central Rongbuk Glacier, at least 7,000 ft below Mallory's body; the cameras remain missing.

stories.description: The Rohonc Codex has been in the Hungarian Academy of Sciences since 1838 and nobody has read a word of it. Its 792 symbols are too many for an alphabet, and the leading theory is that a notorious 1830s forger wrote the whole thing. #unsolvedmysteries #bizarrehistory #codes

Kalman Nemati counted 792 distinct symbols in 1889, and published readings of the codex as Hungarian, Daco-Romanian and Hindi were all criticised and rejected.

segments.narration: This book has 448 pages and no readable word. Hungary has owned it since 1838 and still cannot open it.
Count Batthyany handed it to the Hungarian Academy of Sciences with his entire library. Eighty-seven drawings sit inside: churches, soldiers, battles.
One scholar counted 792 different symbols. Far too many for an alphabet. Readings in Hungarian, Romanian and Hindi have all been published, and all thrown out. Who fills 448 pages with nothing?
Most Hungarian scholars think somebody did exactly that, deliberately. Samuel Literati Nemes, a dealer who forged manuscripts in the 1830s, has been the suspect since 1866.
The paper is Venetian, made around the 1530s. Not one document ties Nemes to the book, so the best theory anyone has is still a suspicion.

research.summary: The Rohonc Codex is an illustrated manuscript of 448 paper pages, each about 12 by 10 cm, with 9-14 rows of symbols per page and 87 illustrations showing religious, secular and military scenes. It was kept at Rohonc (now Rechnitz, Austria) until 1838, when Count Gusztav Batthyany donated it with his library to the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, where it still is; the only earlier record is a 1743 Batthyany family library catalogue. Kalman Nemati counted 792 distinct symbols in 1889; most appear rarely, so the system may be a syllabary or logographic rather than alphabetic. The paper is most probably Venetian and made in the 1530s, though paper can be used long after manufacture, and Lang suggests a 16th-17th century text. Karoly Szabo proposed in 1866 that Samuel Literati Nemes (1796-1842), a dealer responsible for many forgeries mostly in the 1830s, produced it, and mainstream Hungarian scholarship has long accepted that view, but no evidence directly connects him to the codex. Proposed decipherments by Attila Nyiri (1996, Sumero-Hungarian), Viorica Enachiuc (2002, Daco-Romanian) and Mahesh Kumar Singh (2004, Brahmi-based Hindi) were each criticised; Tokai and Kiraly (2018) argued it is a code system and suggested a probable 1593 date. There is no widely accepted translation or interpretation.

stories.title: Parliament Hung Lime Curtains To Block The River's Smell
stories.description: In the hot summer of 1858 the Thames, London's open sewer, smelled so bad that the Palace of Westminster soaked its curtains in chloride of lime. Parliament funded Joseph Bazalgette's sewers within weeks, and the city never had another cholera outbreak after 1866. #unsolvedmysteries #bizarrehistory #victorianlondon
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's top mature video, France Sent An Army After One Animal In 1765 at 1,446 views, works by naming an institution doing something absurd, so this leads with Parliament hanging lime-soaked curtains rather than with Victorian sanitation.

factual_claims.text: During the summer of 1858 the curtains on the river side of the Palace of Westminster were soaked in chloride of lime to block the smell of the Thames.
London's population had risen to about three million, with roughly 200,000 cesspits and 360 sewers draining into the Thames, and June 1858 shade temperatures averaged 34 to 36 degrees Celsius.
Officials discussed moving the government out of London to Oxford or St Albans during the Great Stink.

Disraeli tabled the Metropolis Local Management Amendment Bill on 15 June 1858 and it became law on 2 August 1858, letting the Metropolitan Board of Works borrow three million pounds; Joseph Bazalgette's scheme included 82 miles of main interceptor sewers.
Bazalgette's system used 318 million bricks and about 1,100 miles of street sewers, and the 1866 outbreak was London's last cholera outbreak.

segments.narration: Parliament soaked its curtains in lime to survive the smell. London, summer 1858. The Thames was the city's open sewer.
Three million people, about two hundred thousand cesspits, and 360 sewers all emptying into the river. Then June hit thirty-six degrees and the water dropped.
Officials seriously discussed moving the government to Oxford, or to St Albans. Nothing concentrates a legislature like a smell it cannot escape.
A bill went in on the fifteenth of June and was law by the second of August. Joseph Bazalgette got three million pounds and built eighty-two miles of interceptor sewers.
It took 318 million bricks and eleven hundred miles of street sewers. London's last cholera outbreak was 1866, and the thing still runs.

research.summary: In July and August 1858 hot, dry weather made the untreated human waste and industrial effluent on the Thames banks in central London unbearable; June 1858 shade temperatures averaged 34-36 C and the sun reached 48 C. London's population had grown from about one million to three million, flushing toilets had multiplied the volume, and around 1856 the city had roughly 200,000 cesspits and 360 sewers draining to the river, whose falling level left raw sewage exposed. Curtains on the river side of the Palace of Westminster were soaked in chloride of lime without success, and officials discussed moving government to Oxford or St Albans. Disraeli tabled the Metropolis Local Management Amendment Bill on 15 June 1858 and it became law on 2 August, letting the Metropolitan Board of Works borrow 3 million pounds repaid by a three-penny household levy over forty years. Joseph Bazalgette, at the Metropolitan Commission of Sewers from 1849 with definitive plans by June 1856, built about 1,100 miles of street sewers feeding 82 miles of main interceptors, using 318 million bricks and 880,000 cubic yards of concrete and mortar, for about 6.5 million pounds against a 2.4 million estimate. Work on the northern system began 31 January 1859; Crossness opened April 1865, the Albert Embankment November 1869, Victoria July 1870, Chelsea July 1874, western drainage 1875. Cholera killed 6,536 in 1831, 14,137 in 1848-49, 10,738 in 1853-54 and 5,596 in 1866; the 1866 outbreak was the capital's last, and the system still operates.

segments.narration: An AI nearly doubled the number of drawings in this desert. Southern Peru, where the Nazca lines run for thirteen hundred kilometres.
They were made by scraping away the reddish pebbles to show the pale ground underneath. Most of the grooves are ten to fifteen centimetres deep.
Two thousand years of wind, almost no rain, and the hummingbird scraped into that plain is still sharp. So what were they actually for?
Not a star chart. Hawkins and Aveni tested the alignments and found the case too weak. The reading now is religious: paths walked in procession, and figures asking for water.

research.summary: The Nazca Lines lie on an arid plateau in southern Peru stretching over 80 km between Nazca and Palpa, about 400 km south of Lima; the combined length of the lines exceeds 1,300 km and the densest concentration is a 10 by 4 km area. More than 70 figures are zoomorphic and hundreds more are lines and geometric shapes; the known count was 358 in 2022. They were made between about 500 BC and AD 500 by removing the reddish iron-oxide-coated pebbles covering the desert to expose pale subsoil; lines are typically 10-15 cm deep and more than half about 33 cm wide. The dry, windless climate and lime-rich subsoil that hardens in morning mist preserved them. Pedro Cieza de Leon described them in 1553; Toribio Mejia Xesspe spotted them in 1927, Paul Kosok flew over in 1940-41 and Maria Reiche advanced the astronomical interpretation. Gerald Hawkins and Anthony Aveni concluded in 1990 that the astronomical evidence was insufficient. Johan Reinhard (1985) linked the lines to water worship, with lines as sacred paths and figures invoking deities for water, and a 2024 study read figurative line-type geoglyphs as planned public architecture tied to pilgrimage, with Masini and Orefici connecting the lines to the Cahuachi temples. A Yamagata University and IBM Research team used AI to shortlist candidates from 1,309 high-potential sites and, in fieldwork from September 2022 to February 2023, confirmed 303 new figurative geoglyphs, announced in 2024; an earlier 2019 project found 143.

Comets speed up because ice boils off and shoves them. But this thing had no tail. No coma. Nothing visible leaving it at all.
One Harvard physicist suggested an alien lightsail. Most astronomers went the other way: nitrogen or hydrogen ice, venting invisibly from inside.

segments.narration: A medieval skull fooled British science for forty-one years. Piltdown, East Sussex. Announced to the Geological Society in December 1912.
They named it Eoanthropus dawsoni. Dawson's dawn-man. Half a million years old, they said, and the missing link happened to be English.
It confirmed exactly what everyone already believed: big brain first. So real African fossils got shelved for decades, because a forgery outranked them.
Then in 1953, fluorine testing broke it apart. Human skull. Orangutan jaw. Chimpanzee teeth, filed flat and stained with iron to match.
A 2016 study traced both Piltdown sites to one orangutan and one man: Charles Dawson, the amateur who found it. Forty years of textbooks, built on a fake.

segments.narration: A B-24 sat intact in the Sahara for fifteen years. Found in 1958, 710 kilometres inland from the Libyan airfield it flew out of.
Guns still loaded. Radio still working. A thermos of tea somebody could have drunk. And not one person aboard, not one parachute.
April 1943. First mission, bombing Naples. Coming home in the dark, they flew straight over their own base and never saw its flares.
Their direction finder couldn't tell a bearing from its exact reverse. So they kept going south for two hours, certain the desert below was sea.
Eight survived the jump and walked north. Five made 130 kilometres. One made over 320. The ninth man was never found.

factual_claims.text: The British Inland Customs Line was ordered connected in 1869 into a continuous barrier of 4,030 kilometres running from the Himalayas to Orissa near the Bay of Bengal.

The line existed to enforce the salt tax and collect sugar duty, and was built from thorny species including Indian plum, babool and prickly pear, reaching 3.7 metres high and 4.3 metres thick in places.
Staff on the customs line peaked at 14,188 men in 1872, and there were 1,727 customs posts in 1869 to 1870.
The line was abandoned on 1 April 1879 after Britain took control of salt production, and standard histories of the period largely omitted it.
In 1998 Roy Moxham located a small raised embankment in Etawah district, Uttar Pradesh, which may be all that remains of the hedge.

segments.narration: A thorn hedge once cut India clean in half. Four thousand kilometres of it, ordered joined up in 1869, Himalayas down to the Bay of Bengal.
It was there to tax salt. Indian plum, babool, prickly pear, grown nearly four metres high and four metres thick in places.
Over fourteen thousand men patrolled it at its peak, through more than seventeen hundred customs posts. All that, to stop smuggled salt.
Then on 1 April 1879, they dropped it. And a barrier the size of a country simply fell out of the history books.
In 1998 a researcher named Roy Moxham found what's left: one low earth embankment in Etawah district.

research.summary: The Inland Customs Line, popularly the Great Hedge of India, was a British customs barrier enforcing the salt tax and sugar duty. Ordered connected in 1869, it ran 4,030 km from the Himalayas to Orissa; by 1878 it included 662 km of good live hedge and about 1,786 km of inferior hedge, dry hedge or stone wall, in places 3.7 m high and 4.3 m thick. Staff peaked at 14,188 in 1872 across 1,727 posts. Abandoned 1 April 1879 and omitted from standard histories; Roy Moxham found a reference in 1995 and traced a surviving embankment in Etawah district in 1998.

stories.title: Pigeons Were Trained To Steer A Missile In 1943
stories.description: B.F. Skinner put up to three trained pigeons in a missile's nose cone, pecking at a projected image of the target to steer it. The military called it eccentric, funded it anyway, then cancelled it in October 1944. #projectpigeon #ww2 #bizarrehistory
stories.editorial_rationale: Beast of Gevaudan scored 1,302 frozen views and 87.7 percent hook hold on an absurd-but-true image stated completely flat, and three pigeons inside a guided missile is exactly that shape.

factual_claims.text: In B.F. Skinner's Project Pigeon, one to three trained pigeons rode in a missile's nose cone and pecked at a projected image of the target to steer it.
Three lenses in the nose projected the target onto a pivoting screen, and angle sensors turned the pigeons' pecks into steering signals for the control surfaces.
In testing, one bird pecked more than 10,000 times in 45 minutes.
The National Defense Research Committee thought the idea eccentric and impractical but contributed 25,000 dollars, and the programme was cancelled on 8 October 1944.
The US Navy revived the work as Project Orcon in 1948 and cancelled it in 1953 once electronic guidance systems proved reliable.

segments.narration: Three pigeons once sat in the nose of a missile. Not as cargo. As the guidance system, pecking at a screen.
Lenses threw the target onto that screen. The bird pecks where the ship is, the screen tilts, sensors read the angle, the missile turns.
And it worked. One pigeon pecked over ten thousand times in forty-five minutes without stopping. Birds don't panic and don't get distracted.
The defence committee called it eccentric and impractical. Then handed over 25,000 dollars anyway, and cancelled the whole thing in October 1944.
The Navy quietly restarted it in 1948 as Project Orcon, and finally killed it in 1953, when electronics got reliable enough.

research.summary: Project Pigeon was B.F. Skinner's WWII pigeon-guided bomb. Three lenses in the nose projected the target onto a pivoting screen with angle sensors; one to three pigeons trained by operant conditioning pecked at the image, moving the screen and generating steering signals. The NDRC considered it eccentric and impractical but contributed $25,000. One bird pecked over 10,000 times in 45 minutes. Cancelled 8 October 1944 in favour of projects with more immediate combat promise; revived by the Navy as Project Orcon in 1948 and cancelled in 1953. Skinner received a 2024 Ig Nobel Peace Prize for it.

verification.note: Wikipedia: one to three pigeons trained by operant conditioning pecked at the projected image. Smithsonian Magazine describes Skinner's nose cone with three screens and three pigeon compartments, held by the National Museum of American History.

verification.claim: Three lenses projected the target onto a pivoting screen whose angle sensors produced steering signals.
verification.note: Wikipedia describes exactly this mechanism: three lenses, a pivoting screen with angle sensors, pecks moving the screen and the sensors sending steering signals to the control surfaces.

verification.note: Wikipedia gives this as the single reported performance data point and reports no accuracy figures, so the narration claims persistence only. 'Birds don't panic' is framing, not a sourced claim.

verification.note: Wikipedia: the NDRC viewed it as 'very eccentric and impractical', contributed $25,000, and the programme was cancelled on 8 October 1944 to avoid delaying projects with more immediate combat promise. Smithsonian Magazine corroborates the $25,000 grant.

verification.note: Wikipedia: revived by the Navy in 1948 as Project Orcon, cancelled again in 1953 after the reliability of electronic guidance systems was proven.

stories.title: Soloists Blind-Tested Strads And Picked The New Violins
stories.description: A 1721 Stradivari sold for 15.9 million dollars, and for three centuries people have hunted the secret of that sound in the wood, the chemicals and the varnish. In 2014 ten soloists played blind, and six chose a modern violin. #stradivarius #violin #mystery

factual_claims.text: The 1721 Lady Blunt Stradivarius sold in London in 2011 for 15.9 million dollars.
Antonio Stradivari made over 1,100 instruments in Cremona, of which about 650 survive.
Proposed explanations for the sound include unusually dense wood grown during the Little Ice Age and chemical treatments such as borax against woodworm.
Jean-Philippe Echard's 2010 study found the varnish was a mix of common Cremonese resin, oil and pigment, with no special ingredients.

In the 2014 Fritz study ten soloists blind-tested six Old Italian violins including five Stradivari against six new ones, six of the ten chose a new violin, and their old-versus-new guesses were close to chance.

segments.narration: One violin sold for 15.9 million dollars in 2011. The Lady Blunt, built by Antonio Stradivari in Cremona in 1721.
He made over eleven hundred instruments. Around 650 still exist, and people have been chasing their secret for three straight centuries.
Dense wood from the Little Ice Age? Borax soaked in against woodworm? A varnish nobody could copy? Every theory got tested properly.
In 2010 the varnish came back as ordinary resin, oil and pigment. Nothing secret in it. So where is the magic hiding?
In 2014, ten soloists played twelve violins blind. Six picked a modern one, and guessing old from new came out roughly a coin flip. Thirty-one right, thirty-three wrong.

research.summary: Stradivari worked in Cremona in the late 17th and early 18th centuries, making over 1,100 instruments of which about 650 survive; the 1721 Lady Blunt sold for $15.9 million in London in 2011. Proposed causes of the sound include Little Ice Age wood density (Maunder Minimum, c. 1645-1750), chemical treatments such as borax, and varnish; Echard's 2010 study found the varnish was common resin, oil and pigment. In the 2014 Fritz et al. PNAS double-blind study, ten soloists compared six Old Italian violins (five Stradivari) with six new ones; six of ten chose a new violin for a hypothetical tour and old-versus-new identification was near chance (31 right, 33 wrong).
